nameStory: The 'adder's-mouth' name comes from the shape of the tiny orchid flowers, which some people think look like a snake's open mouth ready to strike. This particular species is named after long-time botanist Thomas Bayard, who studied plants in the northeastern United States. It's sometimes called Bayard's adder's-mouth orchid in his honor.
description: Appalachian adder's-mouth is a tiny, inconspicuous orchid that most people walk right past without noticing. This delicate plant grows up to about 10 inches tall and usually has just one oval leaf positioned partway up its slender stem. The flowers are so small and green that they blend right into the surrounding vegetation, arranged in a narrow cluster at the top of the plant. Despite being an orchid, it looks nothing like the showy orchids you might see in a florist shop.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny green flowers clustered in a narrow spike at the top, each flower barely 2-3mm across and easily mistaken for small buds or seeds

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Usually just one oval leaf (occasionally two) positioned about halfway up the stem, with smooth edges and parallel veins typical of orchids

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender, upright stem reaching 4-10 inches tall, often appearing fragile and easily overlooked among other forest plants

idTips.label: Base
idTips.description: Stem emerges from a small, bulb-like swelling (pseudobulb) at ground level that feels firm when gently pressed

habitat: Look for this rare orchid in dry, open woodlands and pine barrens at lower elevations throughout New England, though it's most likely to be found in Massachusetts. It prefers sandy or well-drained soils in areas that get dappled sunlight rather than deep shade. You'll often find it growing among low shrubs and grasses in clearings or along woodland edges.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late spring, appearing fresh and bright green as the plant begins its growing season.
seasonality.summer: Blooming occurs in mid to late summer (July-August), when the tiny green flower spike is most visible at the top of the plant.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to go dormant, with leaves yellowing and eventually withering away.
seasonality.winter: Plant is completely dormant underground, surviving as the small pseudobulb buried in the soil with no visible parts above ground.

funFact: This orchid is so rare in New England that it's been spotted fewer than a dozen times by naturalists using the popular iNaturalist app, making it one of the most elusive orchids in the region - you'd have a better chance of spotting some tropical birds than finding this tiny native orchid!
confusionNotes: The tiny green flowers can easily be mistaken for seed heads of grasses or small buds on other plants. The key difference is the orchid's single oval leaf positioned partway up the stem - grasses have narrow leaves that emerge from the base, and most other small woodland plants have very different leaf arrangements.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that New England has native orchids at all, since we tend to think of orchids as tropical greenhouse plants. Our native orchids are typically small, subtle, and green or brownish rather than the bright, showy colors of their tropical cousins.
compareHints: Unlike green adder's-mouth which has a single leaf at the base of the plant, Appalachian adder's-mouth has its leaf positioned higher up on the stem. White adder's-mouth has whitish flowers instead of green ones and tends to grow in wetter, shadier spots. All three species share the same tiny flower size and inconspicuous appearance that makes them challenging to spot in the wild.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Green adder's-mouth differs from white adder's-mouth by its green (rather than white) flowers and typically taller growth.

White adder's-mouth differs from green adder's-mouth by its paler, greenish-white flowers and single leaf that wraps around the stem base, while green adder's-mouth has distinctly green flowers and a single leaf that doesn't wrap the stem.
